name: Zambia
sources: GDP $3.3bn: World Bank NY.GDP.MKTP.CD, series ZMB, 1990 = 3,288,381,797. Down from 3,994,673,161 in 1989 and still falling — real growth was -0.48% in 1990, -0.04% in 1991 and -1.73% in 1992. Zambia had been the second-richest country in sub-Saharan Africa at independence in 1964 and by 1990 its GDP was a third of Zimbabwe's on three-quarters of Zimbabwe's population. The whole of that is copper: the price collapsed in 1975 and never came back in real terms, the ore grades at Nchanga and Mufulira were falling, and nothing had been built beside it.

Population 7.8m: World Bank SP.POP.TOTL, series ZMB, 1990 = 7,786,169. The census of August 1990 counted 7,383,097. Zambia was already among the most urbanised countries in Africa — the Copperbelt and the line of rail — which is why a maize price rise was a political event rather than an agricultural one.

TFP trend 0.001: the lowest figure in this region and close to the floor of the model, and it is meant to be. Zambia in 1990 was fifteen years into a decline it had not adjusted to: ZCCM's mines were decapitalised, the parastatal conglomerate ZIMCO held most of the rest of the formal economy, the IMF programme had been abandoned in May 1987 in favour of a home-grown plan and then quietly resumed in 1989, and no new tradable sector had appeared. Set below Kenya's 0.004 and Tanzania's 0.005 because Tanzania was four years into a recovery and Zambia was not yet into one at all.

Inflation 107%: World Bank FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG, series ZMB, 1990 = 107.02. The context is the whole Zambian year: the government removed the subsidy on mealie meal in June 1990, prices of the staple roughly doubled, students and Copperbelt townships rioted, at least twenty-seven people were killed, and Lieutenant Mwamba Luchembe announced a coup on state radio on 30 June. Kaunda conceded a referendum on multi-party politics in September and then conceded multi-party politics itself in December. None of that is scripted here; what is entered is the price level he was standing on in January.

Interest rate 72%: THE TRANSCRIBED FIGURE IS 35.1% AND THIS IS NOT IT. World Bank FR.INR.LEND, series ZMB, 1990 = 35.10, an administered Bank of Zambia lending rate against consumer prices rising 107% — a real rate of about MINUS 36 points, the deepest financial repression anywhere in this roster and an explicit instrument of the controlled economy rather than an accident. The model cannot hold it: the loader refuses a real rate more than 0.5 from the 0.025 neutral because the demand channel in economy.rs is linear and unbounded in that distance, and 0.35 against 1.07 is 0.745 away. 0.72 is entered as the stand-in on the precedent Poland (0.55/0.30) and Yugoslavia (0.60/0.30) already set in this directory, and it reads 0.025 - (0.72 - 1.07) = 0.375 from neutral. That preserves the sign and the ordering — Zambia opens with the most negative real rate on the board, wider than Yugoslavia's 0.325 — and it does not preserve the magnitude. Said plainly so that nobody later reads 0.72 as a Bank of Zambia print.

Revenue 20.4% of GDP: World Bank GC.REV.XGRT.GD.ZS, series ZMB, 1990 = 20.41. Genuinely sourced, unlike most of this region, and higher than it looks for a poor country because the mines were state-owned and the mineral take ran through the budget.

Military 3.4% of GDP: World Bank MS.MIL.XPND.GD.ZS, series ZMB, 1990 = 3.41, down from 4.20 in 1989. High for an army that never fought a war, and the reason is that Zambia was raided rather than invaded: Rhodesian forces struck ZAPU camps around Lusaka repeatedly until 1979 and South African forces struck ANC houses in Lusaka as late as 1987.

Investment 16% of GDP, split 9 state / 7 private: NOT SOURCED. World Bank NE.GDI.TOTL.ZS has no Zambian entry for 1990, so both the total and the split are brackets rather than transcriptions and are flagged as such. The total is set low — below Tanzania's 18% and less than half Botswana's 37% — because Zambia in 1990 was consuming its capital stock rather than replacing it, which is the finding the mines' falling output records. Weighted toward the state because ZIMCO and ZCCM were the state.

Debt 230% of GDP: World Bank DT.DOD.DECT.GN.ZS, series ZMB, 1990 = 229.54, external debt stocks as a share of GNI. THE HIGHEST FIGURE IN THIS ROSTER by a wide margin — above Jordan's 200%, Zaire's 119% and Tanzania's 107% — and it is not a typo. Zambia carried roughly $7bn of external debt on a $3.3bn economy and was among the most indebted countries in the world per head in 1990. It reached HIPC completion in 2005.

Oil 0.0: no production. Zambia's crude came up the TAZAMA pipeline from Dar es Salaam to the Indeni refinery at Ndola, which is the same logic as the TAZARA railway beside it — infrastructure built at cost to avoid shipping through Rhodesia and South Africa.

Stability 45 and authoritarianism 0.70: stability is set below Zimbabwe's 58 and Nigeria's 35 is below it in turn, which places Zambia as a government with a real administration and no economic answer. UNIP had been the sole legal party since the constitution of December 1972 and Kaunda had run unopposed in a yes/no vote in 1988; the Preservation of Public Security Act allowed detention without trial and was used. Authoritarianism 0.70 is set BELOW Tanzania's 0.72 and well below Kenya's 0.78 for the reason the next two years demonstrate: when Kaunda lost the argument he held an election on 31 October 1991, lost it 76-24, and left State House. A one-party state that can be voted out is not the same object as one that cannot.

Separatism 0.06: Barotseland. Lewanika's kingdom acceded in 1964 under the Barotseland Agreement, which promised the Lozi a large measure of self-government; Kaunda abrogated it by the Local Government Act of 1965 and formally in 1969, and Lozi grievance about it has been continuous ever since without ever becoming an insurgency. Set below Zimbabwe's Matabeleland at 0.08 because Zambia's version never produced a Gukurahundi and never produced a gun.

Military strength 2.5: the Zambian Army was about 16,000 with an air force flying MiG-21s and a small SA-3 network, set level with Zaire's 2.5 and below Kenya's 3. It absorbed Rhodesian and South African raids for fifteen years without once being able to prevent one, which is the honest reading of what that index buys.
